questions.q: What is the maximum number of callouts a single Apex transaction can make, per Salesforce's execution governors?
options: There is no limit on the number of callouts per transaction
questions.explain: Salesforce's Execution Governors and Limits reference sets the total number of callouts (HTTP requests or web service calls) in a transaction at 100.

questions.q: What is the combined cumulative timeout budget shared across all callouts in a single Apex transaction?
questions.explain: All callouts in one transaction share a maximum cumulative timeout of 120 seconds, regardless of how many individual callouts make up that total.

questions.q: What is the core purpose of a Named Credential (or the newer External Credential model)?
options: To define the callout's endpoint and required authentication in an admin-managed record, keeping secrets out of Apex source code
To automatically retry a failed callout indefinitely
To convert a synchronous callout into an asynchronous one
questions.explain: Named Credentials (and the newer External Credentials) exist to keep endpoint and authentication details in a protected, admin-managed setup record rather than hardcoded in Apex, where every developer with code access could read a secret.

questions.q: Why does Apex disallow a synchronous callout from inside a trigger?
options: Because triggers cannot reference Named Credentials

Because a callout that blocks waiting on a third party inside a DML transaction risks a slow or unreachable external system stalling or failing Salesforce's own save, affecting other users on the same transaction threads
Because triggers run with a different, incompatible version of the Apex runtime
Because trigger context variables cannot be passed into a callout
questions.explain: The restriction exists because of the coupling risk: a callout blocking inside a trigger's transaction ties Salesforce's own save to the latency and reliability of an external system, which real incidents have shown can lock up transaction threads under load.

questions.q: What is the recommended fix for a design that wants to call an external API as a reaction to a record save, without risking the save itself?
options: Call the API synchronously but wrap it in a try/catch block
Move the callout off the synchronous save path using asynchronous Apex (such as a Queueable class), so it runs after the save has already committed
Increase the org's API version to bypass the callout limit
Disable all triggers on the object before making the callout
questions.explain: Async Apex (Queueable, or a Platform Event handler) performs the callout after the triggering transaction has already committed, so a slow or failing external system can never block or fail the original save.
